Evidence: CFPB issue spotlight (June 2023): each of the top 10 largest commercial banks has deployed chatbots as part of customer service (CFPB's own review) | Market estimate cited by CFPB, not CFPB-measured: over 98 million users (about 37% of the US population) engaged with a bank chatbot in 2022, projected to reach 110.9 million by 2026 | CFPB describes 'doom loops' of unhelpful responses without an offramp to a human representative, illustrated with quoted consumer complaints, and says chatbot effectiveness wanes as problems grow more complex | Third-party survey cited by CFPB: 80% of consumers who used a chatbot left more frustrated and 78% needed to reach a human
Implication: Any agent that touches disputes, holds or account problems needs an obvious, fast handoff to a human, because blocked recourse is the documented failure regulators already watch for.
Caveats: Describes scripted and early-LLM chatbots, not agents. Complaint excerpts are self-selected and not a rate. The 37% usage and 80%/78% frustration figures are third-party estimates the CFPB cites; their method was not checked. Pre-2024; later CFPB posture not reviewed.

Claim: In a 2024 US probability-sample experiment, only 5% of adults said they use AI for financial decisions and trust in identical financial statements differed by whether AI or a professional was named as the source for three of four statements.
Evidence: FINRA Foundation (SSRS Opinion Panel, 1,033 US adults, Feb 16-19 2024, AAPOR3 response rate 2.4%, MOE 3.6 pts): asked which information sources they use when making financial decisions, 63% named financial professionals, 56% friends and family, 25% financial apps, 5% AI | Half of respondents were told each statement came from AI and half from a financial professional, then asked how far they trusted it; portfolio-allocation statement trusted by 30% (AI) vs 37% (professional) | Stock/bond forecast trusted by about a third either way (34% AI, 33% professional); higher self-rated knowledge trusted the AI version more (48% vs 34%), lower-knowledge less (25% vs 32%) | Group differences ran both ways: Black respondents trusted the homeownership statement more from AI (71% vs 49%) but the savings/debt statement more from a professional (69% vs 48%)
Implication: Customer trust in AI-sourced money information varies by topic, knowledge and group, so one uniform AI label or tone will not fit all customers.
Caveats: FINRA Investor Education Foundation (regulator-affiliated nonprofit, not a vendor). Low response rate, weighted. Statements were hypothetical investing and personal-finance information, not bank service or an agent taking action. Source-attribution manipulation overlaps T6-A. Self-reported AI use likely understates AI embedded in apps.

Claim: In a late-2024 union survey of about 2,200 Australian finance workers, 61% said AI threatens their job and 61% had received no AI training from their employer.
Evidence: Finance Sector Union survey (Nov-Dec 2024, about 2,200 workers across banking, insurance, superannuation and financial planning): 61% feel AI threatens their job, 17% unsure; 68.6% expect a negative impact on job security vs 9.2% positive | 61% had no AI training from their employer; 41% do not feel prepared to work alongside AI (28% unsure); 8% rate their AI understanding very good and 38% low or very low | Only 13% said their employer had discussed AI impacts with them, yet more than three quarters use AI to some extent (46% sometimes or often) | FSU media release (25 Nov 2025) on a follow-up: 36% often use AI (19% in 2024) and 70% see AI as a job-security threat; the release gives no n or field dates
Implication: Plan associate training, early role-by-role conversations and a stated job-security position as part of the agent rollout, because at least one large bank workforce reports none of these.
Caveats: Union-run with an advocacy position; self-selected, non-anonymous (asks name and employer), no weighting described. Australia, not US. Fielded before the agentic wave; asks about AI generally. Release says 60% in 2024 vs 61% in the report. PDF text extracted locally with PyMuPDF.

Claim: US workers' use of AI is rising but more are worried than hopeful about it, and fear of job elimination grew to 18% by early 2026.
Evidence: Pew (5,273 employed US adults, American Trends Panel, Oct 7-13 2024): 52% worried and 36% hopeful about future workplace AI use; 32% expect fewer job opportunities for themselves, 6% more | Pew (5,010 US workers, Sept 2-8 2025): 21% say at least some of their work is done with AI, up from 16% a year earlier; 65% do not use it much or at all | Gallup (23,717 employed US adults, Feb 4-19 2026, MOE 0.9 pts): 50% use AI at work at least a few times a year; 18% say it is very or somewhat likely their job will be eliminated within five years due to AI or automation (23% in AI-adopting organizations) | Gallup indicator (May 2026): among employees in AI-integrating organizations, 36% strongly agree their manager supports team AI use, and those who do are 1.7x as likely to use AI a few times a week or more; daily use is 27% in finance vs 42% in technology
Implication: Expect an anxious rather than neutral associate baseline and give team leaders an explicit role in agent rollouts, since manager support is the measured correlate of use.
Caveats: All US workers, not bank employees; only finance-specific figure is daily use. AI and chatbots generally, not agents. Manager-support link is correlational. Gallup sells workplace consulting, not AI. Question wording paraphrased on the pages, not printed in full. Gallup's two pages report different dates (Feb vs May 2026).

Claim: In a staggered rollout of a generative AI assistant to 5,172 customer-support agents, access raised issues resolved per hour by 15% and was associated with lower attrition, most among agents with under six months' tenure.
Evidence: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (arXiv v2, Nov 2024): 5,172 agents at one firm; productivity up 15% on average, with less experienced and lower-skilled agents gaining most and the most skilled seeing small quality declines | Agents with under 6 months' tenure: about 10 percentage points lower attrition, a 40% decrease from a 25% baseline; significant decreases across skill groups | Customers were more polite and less likely to ask for a manager, which the authors read as an improved experience of work | Average adherence to AI suggestions was 38% (interquartile range 23-50%), rising over time, so agents kept discretion
Implication: An assist-style tool that leaves the associate in control showed retention benefits for new hires, so pilots of agent-assist should measure new-hire attrition, not only handle time.
Caveats: Field data from one software firm, agents mostly in the Philippines, rollout Nov 2020-Feb 2021 on an earlier model; not a bank and not agentic (suggests responses, does not act). Authors warn attrition results may be overstated if access went to agents likelier to stay. Paper also states 35% average adherence elsewhere in the text.

Claim: Explanations of AI recommendations tend to raise acceptance whether or not the AI is right, and reduce overreliance only when they make checking the AI cheaper than doing the task.
Evidence: Bansal et al. (CHI 2021), user studies on three datasets (beer and book review sentiment, LSAT questions) with crowdworkers and an AI about as accurate as humans: AI assistance gave complementary gains but explanations did not add to them, and explanations increased acceptance regardless of correctness | Vasconcelos et al. (CSCW 2023), five studies, N=731 US-located Prolific workers, maze task with a simulated AI: task difficulty (Study 1, N=340), explanation difficulty (Studies 2-3, N=340 and 286), reward (Study 4, N=114) and effort discounting (Study 5, N=76) all shifted overreliance | Vasconcelos: where explanation effort was lower the reduction in overreliance was larger; authors argue earlier null effects reflect explanations that did not lower verification cost
Implication: Design agent rationales as cheap-to-check pointers to source records rather than persuasive narratives, and test whether they raise blind acceptance by reviewers.
Caveats: Lab tasks with paid crowdworkers standing in for reviewers; not bank operations. Bansal explanations were feature highlights, not LLM rationales; Bansal sample sizes not extracted for this row. Per-study effect sizes from Vasconcelos not extracted.

Claim: Cognitive forcing designs reduced following of incorrect AI advice compared with simple explanation displays, but participants rated them least favourably.
Evidence: Buçinca, Malaya and Gajos (CSCW 2021): 199 MTurk participants; three cognitive forcing designs vs two simple explainable-AI designs vs no AI, on a meal carbohydrate-substitution task | On carb-source detection when the AI was wrong, overreliance was 0.64 (simple XAI) vs 0.48 (forcing), d=.36, p=.003; share correct 0.08 vs 0.27, d=.66 | On the overall decision, overreliance difference was not significant (0.30 vs 0.26, d=.12) though share correct rose (0.03 vs 0.09, d=.37) | Designs that cut overreliance most received the least favourable subjective ratings; benefits were larger for people higher in Need for Cognition
Implication: Friction at the point of agent output (reviewer commits a judgement first) is a measurable lever against rubber-stamping, but expect associate pushback and uneven benefit.
Caveats: Low-stakes nutrition task, paid crowd sample, simulated AI; effect clearest on a sub-measure and weaker on the overall decision. Participant location not verified. Text extracted locally with PyMuPDF.

Claim: Showing an AI's per-case confidence calibrated people's reliance on it in a 2020 experiment, but calibration alone did not improve joint decision accuracy.
Evidence: Zhang, Liao and Bellamy (FAT* 2020), Experiment 1: 72 MTurk participants predicting whether income exceeds $50K; participants' own accuracy 65%, AI accuracy 75% on sampled trials | Interaction of showing confidence and AI confidence level on switching to the AI: F(4,256)=15.8, p<.001; trust rose when shown confidence was above 80% and fell when below 60% | Without confidence shown, reliance stayed flat across confidence levels; authors conclude calibration is not sufficient unless humans bring complementary knowledge, and flag problems with local explanations
Implication: Surface agent confidence per case to steer reviewer attention, and check that reviewers hold knowledge the agent lacks, or calibration will not improve outcomes.
Caveats: Small crowd sample; census-style income task, not a bank decision; IBM Research authors. Confidence was a classifier score, which LLM agents do not natively provide in calibrated form. Experiment 2 (n=9) not used.

Claim: Reliance on algorithmic advice depends on control and expertise: letting people adjust an algorithm's forecasts roughly doubled its use, while experts discounted algorithmic advice that lay people over-weighted.
Evidence: Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey (author manuscript): 32% chose the model when they could not change it vs 73% (change-10) and 76% (adjust-by-5), N=145; replication 47% vs 77% and 75%, N=542 | Dietvorst: use did not depend on how much adjustment was allowed (71%, 71%, 68% across adjust-by-10/5/2); those who could modify were later likelier to choose model-only (30% vs 12%) | Logg, Minson and Moore (OBHDP 2019), six experiments: lay people weighted advice more when told it came from an algorithm than a person; appreciation waned when choosing between the algorithm and their own estimate | Logg Experiment 4: 282 lay people and 61 US national security professionals answered all tasks; experts relied less on algorithmic advice, which hurt their accuracy
Implication: Give associates bounded, logged override controls over agent output and plan different onboarding for experienced investigators or underwriters, who are likelier to discount agent recommendations.
Caveats: Low-stakes lab forecasting tasks with MTurk/student samples; traditional statistical models, not agents. Dietvorst file is an undated manuscript, so its publication year is not verified from the source; Dietvorst sample location not checked. Adoption is not the same as calibrated trust, and adjustments can lower accuracy.

Claim: In a 2023 loan-approval study (N=267), explanations raised informational fairness and contestability raised procedural fairness, while human oversight showed no detectable effect.
Evidence: Yurrita et al. (CHI 2023): user study, N=267, high- and low-stakes loan approval scenarios, varying explanations, human oversight and contestability | Explanations contributed to informational fairness perceptions and contestability to procedural fairness; no evidence for an effect of human oversight | Both fairness types raised overall fairness with no interaction; qualitative tensions between information overload and understanding, and between human involvement and timely decisions
Implication: For adverse-action and hold decisions, build a visible way to contest the outcome; stating that a human reviewed it may not move perceived fairness on its own.
Caveats: Abstract-level only: the full-text PDF returned 403, so effect sizes, recruitment platform and participant location are unverified. Hypothetical scenario measuring perceived fairness, not behaviour or appropriate trust. Not an agent.

Claim: In a randomized field experiment on outbound sales calls, telling customers up front that the caller was a chatbot cut purchase rates by more than 79.7%, while undisclosed chatbots sold as well as proficient human callers.
Evidence: Luo, Tong, Fang and Qu, Marketing Science 38(6), 2019: field experiment with more than 6,200 customers randomized to highly structured outbound sales calls from chatbots or human workers | Undisclosed chatbots were as effective as proficient workers and four times as effective as inexperienced workers at producing purchases; disclosure before the conversation reduced purchase rates by more than 79.7% and shortened calls | Mechanism per the abstract: once customers knew the partner was not human they were curt and bought less, seeing the bot as less knowledgeable and less empathetic; the abstract says late disclosure timing and prior customer AI experience mitigate the penalty, without giving a size
Implication: Treat disclosure timing as a variable to test in any customer-facing agent channel, because the measured penalty attached to disclosure before the conversation and the paper reports it can be reduced by later disclosure.
Caveats: Abstract-only read: the INFORMS full text returned 403, so the size of the late-disclosure mitigation is unknown; pre-LLM scripted sales bot, not an agent and not a bank service interaction; field-site country not stated on the fetched page (one author lists a China affiliation); mandatory up-front disclosure rules (EU Art. 50, Utah high-risk) may remove the timing option.

Claim: Resistance to an AI provider weakens when the AI is framed as supporting a human decision-maker or is consulted only after the human forms an independent view, according to two healthcare experiment packages (2019 and 2026).
Evidence: Longoni, Bonezzi and Morewedge, Journal of Consumer Research 46(4), 2019, Study 1 (228 US university students): 39.8% signed up for a stress assessment when a human would do the analysis vs 26.7% when automated (chi-square(1) = 4.4, p = .03) | Same paper, abstract: resistance is driven by uniqueness neglect and is eliminated when care is framed as personalized (Study 7, interaction F(1, 290) = 6.72, p = .01) or when AI only supports rather than replaces a human provider's decision (Study 9) | Schaffernak et al., J Med Internet Res 28:e93172, Aug 2026, two preregistered vignette experiments with German adults (n = 489 and 570): a physician using diagnostic AI lowered trust in the decision vs descriptive AI (5.00 vs 5.37 on a 7-point scale, p = .002) and provider trustworthiness (4.93 vs 5.40, p < .001) | Study 2 of the 2026 paper: the diagnostic-AI trust penalty appeared when the physician reviewed AI output concurrently but not when the physician assessed the case first (interaction for trust t(436) = 2.71, p = .007); willingness to follow advice did not differ significantly
Implication: Where an agent's role is visible to customers, describe and sequence it as a check on a named associate's own judgment rather than as the decision-maker, and test that framing before relying on it.
Caveats: Healthcare, not banking; hypothetical choices and vignettes, not real service; pre-LLM AI in the 2019 paper; the Study 9 support-vs-replace result was verified only from the 2019 abstract (the fetched article text was truncated before its results); not tests of agents executing actions.

Claim: In five MTurk experiments (N = 3,828), people rated algorithmic fund managers as less permitted than humans to make investment decisions, but in an incentivized choice of manager the pooled aversion disappeared until stated performance was made equal.
Evidence: Niszczota and Kaszás, PLoS One 15(9):e0239277, Sept 2020: internal meta-analysis across five studies (N = 3,828) gives robo-investment aversion d = -0.39 [-0.45, -0.32] | Studies 1-3 (n = 466, 1,231, 683; hypothetical permissibility ratings): overall d = -0.25, -0.58 and -0.81, all favouring human managers | Study 4 (n = 705, choice between a real MTurk-recruited human adviser and an actual neural-network algorithm): pooled d = 0.08 [-0.07, 0.23], i.e. no aversion; d = -0.09 (n.s.) for controversial stocks and +0.26 favouring the algorithm for non-controversial stocks | Study 5 (n = 743, human and algorithm told they performed similarly): 57.3% chose the human adviser (chi-square(1) = 16.0, p < .001; d = -0.30)
Implication: Do not treat stated disapproval of AI-made financial decisions as a forecast of behaviour; test agent disclosure with real-stakes choices before concluding it will reduce uptake.
Caveats: Wealth/investment segment, transfer to retail banking is by inference; MTurk samples, participant country not stated in fetched text; compares choosing a human vs an algorithm, not a disclosure manipulation inside one interaction; pre-LLM algorithm.

Claim: In a randomized smart-reply experiment, partners who actually used AI reply suggestions were rated more cooperative, but partners whom participants believed were using them were rated less cooperative and less affiliative.
Evidence: Hohenstein et al., Scientific Reports 13:5487, 2023 (corrected Oct 2023): Experiment 1 randomized 219 participant pairs to have Google smart replies available or not; Experiment 2 randomized 291 pairs to reply-sentiment conditions | Actual partner use of smart replies raised ratings of partner cooperation (IV regression b = 15.66, t(189) = 2.39, p = 0.018) and affiliation (b = 21.79, t(189) = 2.75, p = 0.007), with no effect on dominance | Perceived use (rated 1-5) was associated with lower cooperation (t(92) = -9.89, p < 0.0001) and affiliation (t(92) = -6.90, p < 0.0001) and higher perceived dominance (t(92) = 2.27, p = 0.026), controlling for actual use
Implication: For agent-drafted customer messages, the measured cost comes from recipients suspecting AI, not from AI use itself, so test disclosure wording on recipient reaction rather than assuming silence or labelling is neutral.
Caveats: Peer-to-peer policy chat among crowd participants, not bank service; the suspicion result is correlational (perceived use was measured, not manipulated) and is not a formal disclosure; b values are regression coefficients whose scale units are not stated in the passage read; single-turn reply suggestions, not agents.

Claim: People who use or disclose AI at work are judged less competent and trusted less, in four preregistered PNAS experiments (N = 4,439) and thirteen OBHDP experiments, with the penalty weaker among evaluators who use AI themselves.
Evidence: Reif, Larrick and Soll, PNAS 122(19), May 2025, Study 1 (n = 497): employees imagining an AI tool expected to be seen as less competent (M = 4.72 vs 5.45 for a non-AI tool, p < 0.001) and lazier (3.25 vs 2.72); the study also measured willingness to disclose tool use to managers and colleagues | Reif et al. Study 2 (n = 1,203 observers) rated AI-helped employees lazier and less competent; Study 3 (801 candidates, 1,668 managers in an incentivized hiring task): managers' own AI use moderated hiring of AI-using candidates (interaction b = 0.15, z = 5.80, p < 0.001), with infrequent users favouring non-AI candidates | Reif et al. Study 4 (n = 1,002): for digital tasks, task-fit ratings did not differ between AI-tool and traditional-tool candidates (5.75 vs 5.58, p = 0.112) | Schilke and Reimann, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 188:104405, 2025 (abstract): across 13 experiments actors who disclosed AI use were trusted less than those who did not, regardless of framing or whether disclosure was voluntary or mandatory; the penalty was weaker than being exposed by a third party and was attenuated but not eliminated among evaluators with favourable technology attitudes
Implication: If associates must label or sign off agent-assisted work, make provenance system-generated and routine rather than a personal admission, or expect under-reporting and a peer penalty.
Caveats: Online vignette and hiring-task samples (Cloud Research Connect for Reif; participant country not stated in fetched text); generative AI help used by a person, not labelled agent output; Schilke and Reimann read from abstract pages only (ScienceDirect full text restricted), so sample sizes are not cited; no bank staff.

Claim: In a preregistered UK experiment (N = 1,500), an AI-identity label left a chatbot's persuasive effect statistically equivalent to no label, whereas also disclosing the chatbot's persuasive intent roughly halved it.
Evidence: Preprint arXiv 2608.11794 (Aug 2026): 1,500 UK adults held a short conversation with the same persuasive chatbot on one of 60 policy issues, randomized to no disclosure, an AI-identity disclosure using the EU AI-generated-content label, or that plus disclosure of persuasive intent and instructions | Attitude shift on a 0-100 scale: 12.6 points in control vs 13.1 with the AI-identity label (difference b = 0.06, 90% CI -1.97 to 2.08); the preregistered equivalence test ruled out effects beyond +/-3.7 points (bound d = 0.15, p TOST = .002) | Intent disclosure cut the shift to 6.3 points (b = -6.77 vs control, p < .001, d = 0.25) and raised perceived manipulation (b = 0.62 on a 7-point scale) and counterarguing; the identity label alone left warmth and perceived manipulation equivalent to control
Implication: A bare 'this is AI' label may be behaviourally inert in text conversations, so a bank should not assume a label alone either harms or protects customers; disclosing what the agent is trying to do may matter more.
Caveats: Not peer reviewed; political attitudes, not financial decisions; a single short conversation; content label rather than a human-vs-AI identity swap.

Claim: Crowd raters who could not tell AI from human text in a blind test strongly preferred whichever text was labelled 'Human Generated', including when the labels were deliberately swapped.
Evidence: Zhu, Weissburg, Zhang and Wang, arXiv 2410.03723 (Sept 2024, revised Aug 2025): three tasks (text rephrasing, news summarization, persuasive writing), 600 tasks per experiment, three raters per task, 16,200 evaluations from MTurk workers in Australia, Canada, UK and US | Blind condition: human text preferred in 45.0-48.9% of evaluations, about chance; correctly labelled: 60.8-64.8% preferred the human text | Swapped labels: only 23.5-31.6% preferred the actual human text, so the label rather than the content drove choices; the abstract reports a preference score of over 30% for text labelled human
Implication: Do not assume associates will judge agent-drafted work on its merits once it carries an AI tag; test label wording and placement with real associates before rollout.
Caveats: Preprint, peer-review status not confirmed; raters had no stake in the output; short prose, not operational actions or case decisions; not bank staff.

Claim: EU AI Act Article 50, as published in 2024, requires providers to design AI systems that interact directly with people so those people are told they are dealing with an AI, at the latest at first interaction, applying from 2 August 2026.
Evidence: Art. 50(1), Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: providers must ensure systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so the person is informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person | Art. 50(5): the information must be clear and distinguishable, given at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure, and meet accessibility requirements; Art. 50(2): providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark outputs in machine-readable form as artificially generated | Art. 50(4): deployers must disclose deep fakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless the text has had human review or editorial control; Art. 50(6): without prejudice to Chapter III high-risk duties and other Union or national transparency law | Art. 113 (original text): the Regulation applies from 2 August 2026, with Chapters I-II from 2 February 2025, Chapter III Section 4, V, VII, XII and Art. 78 from 2 August 2025, and Art. 6(1) from 2 August 2027; Art. 50 falls under the general 2 August 2026 date
Implication: Any EU-facing customer channel run by an agent needs a first-contact AI notice built in by the provider, and any generated customer-facing content needs a machine-readable marking path.
Caveats: Only the original 2024 Official Journal text was read; later amendments (including a reported 2026 Digital Omnibus change to timing or a grace period for Art. 50(2)) are not verified and may apply, so check the consolidated text; EU only; duties fall mainly on providers, so a bank using a vendor agent depends on the vendor's build.

Claim: Utah SB 226 (effective 7 May 2025) requires a supplier using generative AI in a consumer transaction to disclose it only when a person clearly and unambiguously asks, but requires regulated-occupation providers to disclose proactively in high-risk interactions, which include collecting financial data or giving financial advice or services.
Evidence: Utah Code 13-75-103(1) as enacted by SB 226 (2025, enrolled): a supplier must disclose that the individual is interacting with generative AI and not a human if the individual asks or prompts; the prompt must be a clear and unambiguous request | 13-75-103(2)-(3): an individual providing services in a regulated occupation must prominently disclose generative AI use in a high-risk AI interaction, verbally at the start of a verbal interaction and in writing before a written one; 13-75-101(5) defines high-risk to include collection of financial data and personalized recommendations relied on for significant decisions, including financial advice or services | 13-75-104 safe harbor: no enforcement action if the AI clearly and conspicuously discloses at the outset and throughout the interaction that it is generative AI, is not human, or is an AI assistant; 13-75-102: AI having made the statement or taken the act is not a defence to a consumer protection violation | 13-75-105: administrative fine up to $2,500 per violation; 63I-2-213 amended so the AI Policy Act (Title 13 Chapter 72) repeals 1 July 2027 instead of 1 May 2025; SB 226 repealed 13-2-12
Implication: Adopting the safe-harbor pattern (disclose AI status at the outset and throughout) is a simpler multi-state posture for customer-facing agents than relying on an on-request trigger.
Caveats: Enrolled bill read, not the current codified text, so 2026-session amendments are unchecked; the bill defines generative AI as conversational systems that simulate human conversation, so applicability to background agents that do not converse is unclear; whether a bank or its staff fall within a 'regulated occupation' was not resolved.

Claim: Colorado SB 26-189, signed 14 May 2026, repealed and reenacted the state's 2024 AI Act part as a notice-and-rights regime for automated decision-making technology in consequential decisions, including financial or lending services, effective 1 January 2027, and the 2024 text's general 'you are interacting with an AI system' duty does not appear in it.
Evidence: SB 24-205 (2024, signed) section 6-1-1704: on and after 1 Feb 2026, a deployer or developer of an AI system intended to interact with consumers must disclose to each consumer that they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious to a reasonable person | SB 26-189 section 1 repeals and reenacts Part 17; covered domains include a financial or lending service; new 6-1-1704(1) requires a clear and conspicuous notice before covered ADMT is used to materially influence a consequential decision, and (3) requires a plain-language description of the ADMT's role within 30 days after an adverse outcome | 6-1-1704(6): a creditor giving ECOA/Regulation B (and where applicable FCRA) notices can satisfy the duty through those notices, which may include a brief statement that covered ADMT was used; 6-1-1703: deployers keep compliance records for at least three years | SB 26-189 section 5: takes effect 1 January 2027 and applies to decisions made on or after that date; the legislature bill page shows status Became Law, Governor signed 05/14/2026
Implication: For credit decisions an agent materially influences, plan a point-of-interaction ADMT notice and a 30-day adverse-outcome explanation that piggyback on existing adverse action notices, plus three-year decision records.
Caveats: Whether the 2024 disclosure duty ever operated between its 1 Feb 2026 date and the 2027 replacement is not established: a 2025 delay bill and an April 2026 court stay were reported only in secondary sources and are not relied on; Attorney General rules due by 1 Jan 2027 not reviewed; covers decisions, not whether a chat counterparty is human.

Claim: The CFPB's June 2023 issue spotlight on chatbots found all ten largest US commercial banks used chatbots and identified missing routes to a human and human-like bot presentation as consumer risks, without creating an AI-disclosure rule.
Evidence: CFPB, Chatbots in Consumer Finance, 6 June 2023: its review found each of the top 10 commercial banks had deployed chatbots in customer service; it cites an estimate that over 98 million users, about 37% of the US population, engaged with a bank chatbot in 2022 | It describes 'doom loops' with no offramp to a human representative and says the limits of a chatbot and lack of human access may not be apparent when a customer opens a relationship; it notes some bank chatbots have human names | It warns that conversational agents often present as human-like, which may lead users to overestimate capabilities and share more information than in a web form, in the context of impersonation and phishing bots, and quotes consumer complaints about not reaching a human
Implication: Pair any notice that the counterparty is automated with a visible, working route to a human, since the CFPB framed the missing route, not the bot itself, as the harm.
Caveats: Issue spotlight, not a rule or supervisory expectation; the 37% figure is a third-party estimate the CFPB cites; 2023, mostly rule-based and early LLM chatbots, not agents; the current CFPB's 2025-2026 posture on the spotlight was not checked.

Claim: The FCA-published Mills Review (July 2026) says the UK does not currently define agent identity or require agent verification, lists identity, delegation and liability attribution as unfinished building blocks for agentic finance, and does not set an AI-disclosure rule in the passages read.
Evidence: Mills Review (FCA, July 2026): the UK does not currently define agent identity or require agent verification and has no registry of AI agent operators, so an agent initiating a payment or application reaches a firm with no verified identity and no way to distinguish it from an impersonator | Building blocks for agentic finance are listed as data, identity, authorisation and delegation, payments, liability attribution, and supervision and audit at scale; it notes payments firms developing agent tokens and records to trace the agent, the consent and the transaction | It says AI interfaces can personalise journeys in ways that reduce transparency, making auditability, explainability and clear consent points more important, and flags personalised deceptive design as a distinctive risk | Yonder survey for the Review (5,026 UK adults): 36% would use assistive AI, 30% AI that acts with permission, and 20% fully autonomous AI
Implication: Expect UK supervision of agents to run through consent, identity and accountability, so record who authorised an agent, under what mandate, and what it did on a customer's behalf.
Caveats: Non-US; an independent review with recommendations, not binding rules; the document (about 358k characters) was searched by keyword, not read in full; survey figures are stated intentions, not behaviour.

Claim: Agent identification, delegation and audit logging are being specified in 2025-2026 only through drafts and whitepapers (a NIST NCCoE draft concept paper, an IETF individual Internet-Draft and an OpenID Foundation whitepaper), none of which is an adopted standard.
Evidence: NIST NCCoE draft concept paper (Feb 2026; comment period 5 Feb to 2 Apr 2026) on software and AI agent identity and authorization: focus areas include access delegation linking user identities to agents for accountability, and logging that links agent actions to the non-human identity | Its open questions include how an agent proves authority for a specific action, how 'on behalf of' delegation works, how to bind agent and human identity for human-in-the-loop authorization, and how agents can log actions and intent in a tamper-proof, verifiable way | IETF draft-klrc-aiagent-auth-01 (30 Mar 2026; authors from Defakto Security, AWS, Zscaler, Ping Identity and OpenAI) says audit events must record at minimum the authenticated agent identifier, delegated subject, resource or tool, action and authorization decision, and timestamp with correlation identifier; datatracker marks -01 as an older version now 'Replaced', with no formal IETF standing, expiring 1 Oct 2026 | OpenID Foundation whitepaper 'Identity Management for Agentic AI' (arXiv 2510.25819, 29 Oct 2025) sets out an agenda on agent-centric identity, access control and delegated authority
Implication: Give each internal agent its own identity tied to a named delegating human or owner and a tamper-evident action log now, with a schema that can map onto OAuth, WIMSE or OpenID work later, since no settled standard exists to point to.
Caveats: Drafts that pose questions and create no obligations; the IETF -01 draft is superseded and its replacement was not fetched; several IETF authors work for vendors selling identity or agent products; these address machine identity inside systems, not telling customers or associates that an agent acted.

Claim: Chan et al. (FAccT 2024) propose agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logs as three measures to make AI agents visible, and state that they are not advocating immediate implementation.
Evidence: Chan et al., 'Visibility into AI Agents', arXiv 2401.13138 (Jan 2024, v6 May 2024), accepted to ACM FAccT 2024: assesses agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logging, each with implementations that vary in intrusiveness and informativeness | Identifier design choices include which actors can see it; the paper's example is a financial transaction where an agent identifier could be visible to the bank, the counterparty or the bank API provider; per-instance identifiers may need cryptographic methods such as software attestation | Identifiers could link to an 'agent card' covering evaluation results of the underlying system and deployment details such as goals; the authors stress further study of privacy and power-concentration costs before implementation
Implication: Decide explicitly who sees an agent's identifier and log, and at what granularity (associate, supervisor, auditor, counterparty, customer), because each audience trades accountability against privacy.
Caveats: Conceptual proposal with no empirical test or user study; written by AI-governance researchers, not about a bank deployment.
